name: Hikimayu (eyebrow shaving and repainting)

lead: Hikimayu, meaning pulled eyebrows, was a pre-modern Japanese cosmetic practice in which women plucked or shaved their brows and painted smudge-like ones high on the forehead. Combined with white powder, it gave an elongated forehead and a pale, ethereal face that signalled refinement.

It began in the 8th century with Chinese court fashion, took its distinct Japanese form in the Heian period, and by the Edo period marked married women. The government banned it in 1870, and it survives today in Noh, kabuki, film and festivals.

paras: Practitioners removed the natural eyebrows by plucking or shaving, then drew the new ones with haizumi, a powdered ink made from soot of sesame or rapeseed oil, over a base of white oshiroi powder.
Removing brows has no special modern hazard beyond ordinary plucking or shaving skin irritation. The practice itself is historical and was prohibited by the Meiji government in 1870.

angle.text: The brows were deliberately relocated to change facial proportion and pair with white powder. It is a historical example of reshaping the face with makeup.

lead: Hikimayu (引眉) was a pre-modern Japanese cosmetic practice in which women removed their natural eyebrows and painted "smudge-like" ones on the forehead [1]. It created an elongated forehead and, together with white powder, a pale, stylised face that carried ideals of elegance and status [1][2].

Aristocratic women at the Kyoto court plucked or shaved their brows and drew new ones with haizumi, a powdered ink made from soot of sesame or rapeseed oil [1]. Over time the fashion spread to married women, and for a time men of the court [1].
infobox: Japan; adopted from Chinese court practice, 8th century [1]

paras: Hikimayu involved plucking or shaving the natural brows and drawing high ovals on the forehead [1]. It was paired with oshiroi white powder, and removing brows may have made powder easier to apply [1]. Noh masks for young female roles, from the 14th century, often show hikimayu brows [1].

The practice appeared in the 8th century as the court adopted Chinese customs, with brows painted in arc shapes as in China [1]. In the Heian period (794-1185), as Japanese culture moved away from Chinese models, faces were painted more thickly and brows drawn as higher ovals [1]. One unproven theory links the style to long loose hairstyles that made the forehead look too prominent [1]. In the Edo period (1603-1867) it became associated with married women, together with teeth blackening (ohaguro) [1]. In 1870, in the Meiji era, the government banned hikimayu and ohaguro as inappropriate for modern society [1].

Hikimayu persists in Noh and kabuki, occasional festivals and period films, including Rashomon, Ugetsu and Ran [1]. It is mentioned in The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book [1]. Grokipedia's account also describes ukiyo-e depictions by artists such as Utamaro [2].
